title: A glow stick makes light with almost no heat, and a dye decides its colour

cover.alt: A hand holding a round glass flask of liquid that glows bright red against a dim lab bench.

body: Bending a glow stick breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide into a liquid holding an oxalate ester and a fluorescent dye. The two react to form a fragile, energy-packed molecule, 1,2-dioxetanedione, which falls apart into carbon dioxide and hands its energy to the dye. The dye gives that energy out as light, with very little heat: this is **chemiluminescence**, light made directly by a reaction. The chemistry is the same whatever the colour; the dye’s molecular structure is what decides whether the stick glows blue, green, orange or red.

slides.alt: A hand swirls a round glass flask of reddish liquid on a lab bench. The liquid lights up and glows bright red, casting red light onto the fingers holding the flask.
slides.caption: Hydrogen peroxide meets oxalyl chloride and a red dye, rhodamine, in a flask: a cousin of glow-stick chemistry. It glows bright enough to light up the hand holding it.

slides.question: What happens if you put a glowing glow stick in the freezer?
options: It lasts longer but glows dimmer
slides.explanation: Cold slows the reaction, so the light is dimmer but lasts longer. Warming the stick does the opposite: brighter, for a shorter time.
